title: Soft Mixture of Quantum Experts for Hybrid Quantum-Classical Learning
authors: Valeria Repetto, Romina D'Aurizio, Piero Farinelli
abstract: Quantum Machine Learning (QML) has attracted increasing interest as a possible route to construct feature representations that are difficult to reproduce with classical models. However, near-term QML architectures based on trainable parametrized quantum circuits remain affected by limited hardware resources, noise, and severe optimization difficulties such as barren plateaus. In this work we propose Soft-MoQE, a Soft Mixture of Quantum Experts architecture that replaces variational quantum training with the input-dependent selection and combination of fixed quantum feature maps. The model is composed of a heterogeneous pool of non-trainable quantum circuits, each defining a distinct embedding, and a classical gating network that learns how to weight these embeddings for each data point. We benchmark Soft-MoQE on three PCA-reduced tasks: MNIST parity, MNIST 10-class, and FashionMNIST. Soft-MoQE outperforms the single best expert, the uniform average of all experts and a linear baseline, achieving task-dependent performance comparable to that of a trainable quantum neural network, without optimizing any quantum parameter and with a quantum training cost that is lower by orders of magnitude. The analysis of the class- conditioned expert usage shows that the learned routing combines a few experts for each input, with a selection that depends on the class. These results support the learned routing among fixed quantum circuits as a trainability-aware design principle for hybrid QML.

infographic.key_insight: Soft-MoQE learns input-dependent mixtures of fixed quantum feature maps, achieving competitive performance without training quantum parameters.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Moving trainable components to a classical gating network reduces quantum training cost and avoids quantum-parameter optimization difficulties.
method: Build a heterogeneous pool of fixed quantum circuits that produce distinct feature embeddings.
Train a classical gating network to weight expert embeddings for each input.
Combine embeddings through soft, input-dependent routing.
infographic.evidence_signal: On PCA-reduced MNIST parity, MNIST 10-class, and FashionMNIST, Soft-MoQE outperformed the best single expert, uniform expert averaging, and a linear baseline, with task-dependent performance comparable to a trainable quantum neural network and orders-of-magnitude lower quantum training cost.
infographic.watch_item: Results are limited to PCA-reduced benchmarks; robustness to hardware noise and scaling to larger inputs remain unestablished by the abstract.
infographic.paper_title: Soft Mixture of Quantum Experts for Hybrid Quantum-Classical Learning

title: Ising-Encoded Computational Homogenization: Stress as a Quantum Observable
authors: Mourad Halla, Suvranu De
abstract: Computational homogenization requires repeated solutions of representative volume element (RVE) problems to determine the effective response transferred to the macroscale, including the homogenized stress. Here, we develop a basis-encoded, energy-based variational quantum formulation for linear-elastic computational homogenization. The reduced finite-element energy of the RVE is expressed as a quadratic unconstrained binary optimization (QUBO) problem and mapped to an Ising Hamiltonian, whose ground state represents the equilibrium fluctuation field on the encoding grid. Using the Hellmann--Feynman theorem, differentiation of the strain-dependent Hamiltonian with respect to the prescribed macroscopic strain yields stress observables whose expectation values recover the conventional volume-averaged homogenized stress. A key structural result is that, although the equilibrium Hamiltonian is two-local, the stress observables are one-local. In linear elasticity, the two-qubit coupling coefficients are independent of macroscopic strain, hence, differentiation eliminates all two-qubit coupling terms, leaving only identity and single-qubit Pauli-$Z$ operators. These observables are diagonal in the same computational basis as the Ising Hamiltonian and can therefore be evaluated from the same computational-basis measurements used for the energy. Consequently, the homogenized stress can be obtained directly from the optimized quantum state using the same computational basis measurements as the Ising Hamiltonian, without requiring reconstruction of the microscopic displacement field or an additional measurement basis. Ground states are approximated using the variational quantum eigensolver (VQE), and the formulation is demonstrated on a two-dimensional periodic RVE.

infographic.key_insight: A two-local Ising formulation of linear-elastic homogenization yields one-local stress observables, allowing effective stress to be read from the same computational-basis measurements used for energy.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The formulation enables direct extraction of homogenized stress for multiscale mechanics without reconstructing the microscopic displacement field or adding a measurement basis.
method: Encode the reduced finite-element RVE energy as a QUBO and map it to an Ising Hamiltonian.
Approximate equilibrium ground states with a variational quantum eigensolver (VQE).
Differentiate the strain-dependent Hamiltonian using Hellmann–Feynman theory to obtain stress observables containing only identity and single-qubit Pauli-Z terms.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports a demonstration on a two-dimensional periodic RVE but provides no quantitative accuracy, hardware performance, or scaling results.
infographic.watch_item: Finite encoding resolution and approximate VQE convergence can affect stress accuracy; the abstract does not establish a computational advantage.
infographic.paper_title: Ising-Encoded Computational Homogenization: Stress as a Quantum Observable

title: Parallel transversal entangling gates for fault-tolerant trapped-ion quantum computing
authors: Katrin Bolsmann, Alan Kahan, Alejandro Bermúdez, Markus Müller
abstract: Fault-tolerant quantum computing requires high-fidelity entangling gates that can be implemented efficiently across multiple qubit pairs. We present a scheme for simultaneous pairwise entangling operations, i.e., a transversal controlled-$Z$ gate, across neighboring wells in a double-well trapped-ion architecture. A tailored dynamical decoupling scheme suppresses unwanted couplings with a pulse count that scales quadratically with the number of ions. We show that incorporating a genuine geometric cancellation reduces the pulse count and, for selected register sizes, allows the parallel operation to be completed faster than an equivalent sequence of two-qubit gates while requiring a significantly smaller two-photon Rabi frequency. We assess the experimental feasibility of the protocol by analyzing the impact of decoherence and crosstalk arising from laser wave-vector misalignment. To gain insight into the robustness of fault-tolerant protocols against realistic imperfections of the proposed transversal gate scheme, we investigate how crosstalk-induced gate errors affect the fault-tolerant preparation of a logical Bell state between two $[[4,1,2]]$ quantum-error-detection code blocks. These results highlight the potential of transversal entangling gates as a building block for trapped-ion-based scalable fault-tolerant quantum error correction.

infographic.key_insight: Parallel pairwise entangling gates across neighboring trapped-ion wells could enable efficient transversal controlled-Z operations for fault-tolerant quantum computing.
infographic.engineering_relevance: For selected register sizes, geometric cancellation can make parallel gates faster than sequential two-qubit gates while requiring a substantially lower two-photon Rabi frequency.
method: Implement simultaneous pairwise entangling operations in a double-well trapped-ion architecture.
Suppress unwanted couplings using tailored dynamical decoupling with quadratic pulse-count scaling.
Incorporate geometric cancellation to reduce the required pulse count.
infographic.evidence_signal: The study analyzes decoherence and laser-misalignment crosstalk, then evaluates crosstalk-induced errors in fault-tolerant logical Bell-state preparation using two [[4,1,2]] code blocks.
infographic.watch_item: Performance remains sensitive to decoherence and laser alignment, and the reported speed advantage applies only to selected register sizes.
infographic.paper_title: Parallel transversal entangling gates for fault-tolerant trapped-ion quantum computing

title: Beyond Corpus-Driven Imitation: Evolving Musical Mindsets in the Agentic Orchestra via Quantum Reinforcement Learning
authors: Eduardo Reck Miranda, Moein Fahmideh Vatandoost
abstract: This paper presents a framework for computer-aided music composition and performance based on quantum reinforcement learning and multi-agent interaction. We introduce the agentic orchestra, where musical agents evolve distinct mindsets through trial-and-error engagement with a musical environment, rather than through training on large datasets. The agents are implemented as parameterised quantum circuits. They evolve distinct compositional behaviours, referred to as mindsets. This enables the exploration of musical decision spaces using quantum superposition and entanglement within a hybrid quantum-classical loop. We present two complementary agent architectures: atomistic agents, which process pitch and rhythm independently, and holistic agents, which handle pitch and duration as unified note events. Mindsets are shaped through musically grounded reward functions, which can be combined and weighted to develop different mindsets across agents. The resulting system positions quantum computing agents less as autonomous composers and more as adaptive musical partners, each developing its own musical personality through interaction rather than imitation. Demonstrations show how agents generalise their learned behaviour to previously unseen material, operating in interactive and offline batch modes using MIDI-encoded music. While quantum computers are still in development, experiments conducted on IBM quantum hardware confirmed that musically meaningful learning is achievable with existing quantum computers. For composers and performers, the agentic orchestra opens new possibilities for emergent, process-oriented musical creativity, offering a scalable foundation for quantum computer-aided music composition as quantum computing technology continues to advance.

infographic.key_insight: Quantum reinforcement learning lets musical agents develop distinct compositional mindsets through rewarded interaction rather than imitation of large music corpora.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The framework offers a hybrid quantum-classical approach to adaptive MIDI-based composition and performance with multiple musical agents.
method: Represent musical agents with parameterised quantum circuits in a reinforcement-learning loop.
Use atomistic agents for separate pitch and rhythm decisions, or holistic agents for unified pitch-duration events.
Combine and weight musically grounded rewards to shape distinct agent behaviours.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports generalisation to unseen musical material, interactive and offline MIDI demonstrations, and musically meaningful learning on IBM quantum hardware.
infographic.watch_item: The abstract provides no quantitative benchmarks or evidence of advantage over classical reinforcement learning, leaving comparative performance and scalability unresolved.
infographic.paper_title: Beyond Corpus-Driven Imitation: Evolving Musical Mindsets in the Agentic Orchestra via Quantum Reinforcement Learning

title: CAVQS: Context-Aware Variational Quantum Circuit Synthesis via Unitary Redistribution and Dynamic Reconstruction
authors: Zhilong Liu, Xiangzhen Zhou, Yunqi Huang, Xin Hong, Pengcheng Zhu, Fanxu Meng
abstract: Variational quantum circuit synthesis jointly searches circuit structure and continuous parameters to reduce costly two-qubit gates, but block-based workflows typically instantiate blocks independently, limiting simplification across block boundaries. Moreover, fully unitary synthesis does not exploit opportunities created by permitted output measurements and classical feedforward. We present CAVQS, a context-aware variational synthesis framework that combines unitary redistribution and dynamic reconstruction. First, CAVQS uses QR decomposition to transfer unitary factors between overlapping blocks, preserving the overall transformation while reshaping local synthesis targets to enable cross-block reductions. Second, for blocks that precede permitted terminal measurements, CAVQS constructs ancilla-free dynamic implementations with a CNOT-budgeted pre-measurement search and analytic branch-unitary construction, thereby minimizing expected CNOT cost. Across random-circuit targets, CAVQS reduces mean two-qubit gate counts by 28.79%-42.52%, 2.05%-52.62%, and 30.51%-74.64% relative to QFAST, SQUANDER, and Fast-USYN, respectively, on common successful instances. On 4--6-qubit quantum algorithm benchmarks, the corresponding reductions are 27.27%-36.77%, 20.65%-69.10%, and 36.31%-71.88%, respectively.

infographic.key_insight: CAVQS reduces two-qubit gate counts by optimizing across circuit-block boundaries and exploiting permitted terminal measurements with classical feedforward.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Lower two-qubit gate counts could reduce execution cost and noise exposure, while dynamic implementations require measurement and feedforward support.
method: Redistribute unitary factors between overlapping blocks using QR decomposition while preserving the overall transformation.
Search for ancilla-free dynamic implementations before permitted terminal measurements under a CNOT budget.
Construct branch unitaries analytically to minimize expected CNOT cost.
infographic.evidence_signal: On common successful random-circuit instances, mean two-qubit gate reductions span 2.05%–74.64% across three baselines; on 4–6-qubit algorithm benchmarks, reported reductions span 20.65%–71.88%.
infographic.watch_item: Comparisons on common successful instances do not establish overall synthesis success rates, and dynamic-circuit latency may offset gate savings.
infographic.paper_title: CAVQS: Context-Aware Variational Quantum Circuit Synthesis via Unitary Redistribution and Dynamic Reconstruction

title: A measurement-free quantum error correction protocol for superconducting cavities
authors: Q. Rumman Rahman, S. M. Girvin, D. K. Weiss
abstract: The realization of large-scale quantum computation will require quantum error correction (QEC). One way to reduce the demands placed on QEC is to correct dominant physical errors at a lower level before passing the remaining errors to an outer code. Recently, Krastanov et al. [Nat. Commun. 12, 191 (2021)] proposed a measurement-free error-correction protocol based on coherent control of photonic modes that corrects for photon loss. Here, we adapt this approach to a circuit quantum electrodynamics (cQED) architecture using three superconducting microwave cavities coupled by Josephson-junction-based nonlinear elements. We encode the logical qubit in the lowest-order binomial code of one cavity, while the two other cavities serve as ancillas. Using numerical simulations with experimentally realistic parameters, we demonstrate that our protocol can correct single-photon loss with 99% fidelity. Furthermore, we optimize the waiting time between successive rounds of error-correction, and show that the logical lifetime can be extended by a factor of 1.2-1.8 relative to the unprotected Fock $\{|0\rangle, |1\rangle\}$ encoding, surpassing break-even performance. Our work highlights the potential of gate-based, measurement-free QEC for fault-tolerant quantum computing.

infographic.key_insight: A measurement-free protocol corrects single-photon loss in a superconducting cavity and extends simulated logical-qubit lifetime beyond an unprotected encoding.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Coherent, cavity-level error correction could reduce the error burden on an outer quantum error-correcting code without requiring syndrome measurements.
method: Encode a logical qubit in one cavity using the lowest-order binomial code.
Use two ancillary cavities and Josephson-junction-based nonlinear couplings for coherent error correction.
Optimize the waiting time between correction rounds.
infographic.evidence_signal: Numerical simulations with experimentally realistic parameters show 99% single-photon-loss correction fidelity and a 1.2–1.8× logical-lifetime gain over an unprotected Fock {|0⟩, |1⟩} encoding.
infographic.watch_item: The reported gains are simulation-based; experimental performance must be validated under hardware imperfections.
infographic.paper_title: A measurement-free quantum error correction protocol for superconducting cavities

title: Topological Quantum Reservoir Computing
authors: Zhi-Lei Zhang, Lianxiang Cui, C. P. Sun, Kohei Nakajima, Kazuyuki Aihara
abstract: Scaling universal quantum computation and implementing quantum machine learning with protected logical qubits remain challenging. To harness the computational potential of existing fault-tolerant quantum platforms, we introduce topological quantum reservoir computing, a novel approach using protected degrees of freedom for storage and the host system's intrinsic dynamics for information processing. Using a one-dimensional Kitaev chain, we show how long-lived Majorana edge modes and fast bulk responses support these complementary functions within the same many-body system. We identify the tradeoffs governing access to protected memory and show how matched interfaces enable programmable writing and interactions enable autonomous information consolidation from the bulk to the edge. These mechanisms improve performance on tasks requiring long-term retention of temporal information. Our results establish topology as a new resource for quantum reservoir computing and open a route toward near-term quantum computing and quantum machine learning.

infographic.key_insight: Topological quantum reservoir computing combines long-lived Majorana edge modes for memory with fast bulk dynamics for information processing.
infographic.engineering_relevance: This approach could exploit protected quantum degrees of freedom for temporal machine learning without requiring universal logical-qubit computation.
method: Use a one-dimensional Kitaev chain as a quantum reservoir.
Match input interfaces to enable programmable writing into protected memory.
Use interactions to autonomously consolidate information from the bulk into edge modes.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports improved performance on tasks requiring long-term temporal retention, but provides no numerical metrics or benchmark details.
infographic.watch_item: Accessing protected memory introduces tradeoffs, and the abstract does not establish experimental hardware feasibility.
infographic.paper_title: Topological Quantum Reservoir Computing

title: Quantum Annealing with a Quantum Neural Network: Width of Annealing Matters
authors: Mojtaba Asadollahi, Danial Khajehzadeh, Abolfazl Ramezanpour
abstract: Quantum annealing is a promising quantum algorithm for dealing with computationally hard optimization problems. Currently available hardware can implement the algorithm for a significant class of Hamiltonian problems. However, its performance is especially limited in discontinuous quantum phase transitions, where the energy gap shrinks exponentially with system size. In this paper, we introduce an extension of quantum annealing to a quantum neural network and study its performance in a number of prototypical optimization problems. In particular, we observe that already a random quantum annealing network of width W = 2 can exponentially reduce the number of evolution layers or depth of the annealing process in the quantum search problem. By tuning the network parameters the search problem can be solved with exponentially small errors by a quantum perceptron of depth L = 1 and width W = 2. The findings show that width of a quantum annealing network is critical to enhance the success probability of the algorithm by providing a larger and learnable evolution space for the annealing process.

infographic.key_insight: A quantum annealing network with width W = 2 can dramatically improve quantum search, highlighting width—not just depth—as a key design parameter.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Wider, learnable evolution spaces may reduce required annealing depth, motivating quantum optimization architectures that balance width and depth.
method: Extend quantum annealing to a quantum neural network.
Study random and parameter-tuned networks on prototypical optimization problems.
Evaluate how network width and depth affect quantum search performance.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports an exponential depth reduction for random W = 2 networks in quantum search and exponentially small errors for a tuned perceptron with L = 1 and W = 2.
infographic.watch_item: The abstract does not establish hardware feasibility or account for parameter-training costs, so these results should not be read as demonstrated practical speedups.
infographic.paper_title: Quantum Annealing with a Quantum Neural Network: Width of Annealing Matters

title: QuFrame: Pauli Frame Tracking for Fault-Tolerant Quantum Control
authors: Aleksandra Świerkowska, Ilgaz Er, Emmanouil Giortamis, Pramod Bhatotia
abstract: Fault-tolerant quantum computing requires continuous quantum error correction (QEC) to suppress physical noise. While Clifford-only workloads can defer corrections to software post-processing, universal computation breaks this paradigm: executing non-Clifford gates via magic-state gadgets introduces hard, real-time control-flow dependencies on error-corrected measurements. Consequently, the controller must extract syndromes, decode them, and update the Pauli frame in real time, closing the entire QEC loop within a strict $1\,μ\text{s}$ cycle. However, prior proposals on Pauli frame tracking remain largely theoretical, leaving the microarchitectural bottlenecks of tracking, resolving, and synchronizing frame updates across distributed control pipelines unaddressed. To this end, we present QuFrame, a control microarchitecture for real-time Pauli frame tracking that closes the QEC loop within $1\,μ\text{s}$ while sustaining QPU-rate throughput. By introducing QuFrameISA, we cleanly decouple instruction execution from continuous Pauli frame management. Execution is distributed across per-qubit Instruction Resolution Engines (IREs) that resolve instructions against the frame via a single table lookup, while a Pauli Frame Management Unit enables independent, lock-free concurrent commits. To strictly guarantee the $1\,μ\text{s}$ deadline, QuFrame pairs an asynchronous primary decoder with an on-chip fallback decoder that resolves in $144\,\text{ns}$, natively reconciling divergent updates in hardware without degrading logical error rates.

infographic.key_insight: QuFrame is a quantum-control microarchitecture designed to track Pauli frames in real time and close the quantum error-correction loop within 1 μs.
infographic.engineering_relevance: It addresses time-critical control dependencies introduced by non-Clifford magic-state gadgets while sustaining QPU-rate throughput.
method: QuFrameISA separates instruction execution from continuous Pauli frame management.
Per-qubit Instruction Resolution Engines use a single table lookup, while a Pauli Frame Management Unit supports independent, lock-free concurrent commits.
An asynchronous primary decoder is paired with an on-chip fallback decoder and hardware reconciliation of divergent updates.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports 144 ns fallback decoding and a 1 μs QEC-loop deadline without degraded logical error rates, but provides no benchmark or implementation details.
infographic.watch_item: Scalability and timing guarantees need validation under realistic decoder workloads and distributed-control communication delays.
infographic.paper_title: QuFrame: Pauli Frame Tracking for Fault-Tolerant Quantum Control

title: Fault-tolerant quantum processor with minimal external control
authors: Christopher A. Pattison, Jeongwan Haah, John Preskill
abstract: Contemporary classical information processors integrate tens of billions of transistors printed on a chip, yet are fully controlled through comparatively few external wires. This is possible because data flows through hard-coded operations in step with a global clock and is steered by external instructions. Today's solid-state quantum processors are different -- every qubit receives instructions from outside the chip via its own dedicated control line, and error correction adds a further torrent of syndrome data that is transported off-chip. Here we show that the external control of a quantum chip can be greatly simplified. We propose a fault-tolerant architecture for universal quantum computation, inspired by modern classical processors, in which quantum information flows through a fixed, clocked device, propelled by local gates in a planar array. Our quantum processor receives an input stream of classical instructions via a small, constant number of external wires, each attached to a single qubit. Except for those few qubits coupled to external wires, all qubits evolve under a periodically-applied geometrically-local depth-3 circuit, which is fixed at the time the device is fabricated. Assuming a noiseless global clock (so that every operation is applied on schedule, though imperfectly), we establish an accuracy threshold theorem: For physical noise below a universal threshold -- afflicting every gate, measurement, and wire -- a chip with $n$ physical qubits can run any quantum algorithm that uses~$n/{\sf polylog}(n/ε)$ logical qubits, where $ε$ is the error rate per logical gate. Each logical gate takes time~$n/{\sf polylog}(n/ε)$; an alternative design, in which quantum operations remain strictly local and noisy, but on-chip wires broadcast noiseless classical signals instantaneously, reduces the time per logical gate to ${\sf polylog}(n/ε)$.

infographic.key_insight: A proposed fault-tolerant quantum processor replaces dedicated external control of every qubit with a constant number of instruction wires and a fixed, repeating local circuit.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The architecture could reduce quantum-chip control and wiring complexity while retaining universal, fault-tolerant computation.
method: Move quantum information through a planar array using clocked local gates.
Apply a fabrication-fixed, geometrically local depth-3 circuit periodically to nearly all qubits.
Inject classical instructions through a constant number of external wires, each coupled to one qubit.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports a theoretical accuracy-threshold theorem supporting n/polylog(n/ε) logical qubits on n physical qubits, rather than experimental hardware results.
infographic.watch_item: The theorem assumes a noiseless global clock; reducing per-logical-gate time from n/polylog(n/ε) to polylog(n/ε) additionally requires instantaneous, noiseless on-chip classical broadcast.
infographic.paper_title: Fault-tolerant quantum processor with minimal external control

title: Adaptive Hamiltonian Identification via Quantum Reinforcement Learning under Non-Stationary Dynamics
authors: Jawaher Kaldari, Saif Al-Kuwari
abstract: Accurate identification of the Hamiltonian governing a quantum system is important for quantum-system characterization, device calibration, simulation, and reliable operation of quantum hardware. In practical systems, however, the governing dynamics may vary over time because of parameter drift, changing control conditions, or transitions between operating regimes. In this work, we formulate Hamiltonian identification as a quantum reinforcement learning (QRL) problem in which a quantum agent processes sequential quantum-state observations and estimates the governing Hamiltonian parameters. We first consider stationary dynamics using a Vanilla-QRL agent and then introduce a recurrent GRU-QRL architecture to track non-stationary dynamics. The framework is evaluated on transverse-field Ising model systems under stationary dynamics, abrupt Hamiltonian switching, rapidly changing Hamiltonians, random switch locations over longer trajectories, and gradual Hamiltonian drift. We further compare the proposed approach with a Quantum Graph Recurrent Neural Network (QGRNN) baseline and evaluate frozen policies on unseen trajectories. Results show that both approaches accurately reconstruct stationary Hamiltonians, while GRU-QRL provides substantially improved tracking under non-stationary dynamics. These results demonstrate the potential of recurrent QRL as an adaptive system-identification tool for monitoring time-varying quantum systems.

infographic.key_insight: Recurrent quantum reinforcement learning improves Hamiltonian tracking when quantum-system dynamics change over time.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Adaptive Hamiltonian estimation could support quantum-device calibration and monitoring under parameter drift or changing operating conditions.
method: Frame Hamiltonian identification as reinforcement learning from sequential quantum-state observations.
Use Vanilla-QRL for stationary dynamics and a recurrent GRU-QRL architecture for time-varying dynamics.
Compare against a Quantum Graph Recurrent Neural Network baseline and test frozen policies on unseen trajectories.
infographic.evidence_signal: Transverse-field Ising model evaluations cover stationary dynamics, abrupt and rapid switching, randomized switch locations, and gradual drift; the abstract reports accurate stationary reconstruction and substantially improved non-stationary tracking with GRU-QRL.
infographic.watch_item: The abstract does not establish robustness to hardware noise, measurement constraints, or scaling beyond the evaluated Ising systems.
infographic.paper_title: Adaptive Hamiltonian Identification via Quantum Reinforcement Learning under Non-Stationary Dynamics

title: Scaling classical hardware for accurate real-time quantum error correction
authors: Chenyang Jin, Susanne F. Yelin, Andi Gu
abstract: Fault-tolerant quantum computation requires a classical decoder fast enough to process syndrome measurements at the rate at which they are generated, and to return its decisions with low latency. This is most demanding for superconducting processors, whose fast syndrome cycles force a trade-off between decoding speed and accuracy. Decoders fast enough to keep up sacrifice accuracy, which must be compensated for with larger codes and thus additional physical qubits. Here we introduce Rapids, a streaming neural decoder that is both fast and accurate. We achieve this by co-designing the decoder with a field-programmable gate array (FPGA): the network is built from operations that map cheaply onto the device and trained in its integer arithmetic. For the distance-19 surface code, Rapids decodes each round of syndromes in under a microsecond on a single FPGA, fast enough for superconducting processors, and returns its decisions with the low latency that fault-tolerant algorithms require. Its logical error rate is 240 times lower than that of existing real-time hardware decoders. The same design extends to the color code and the [[144,12,12]] bivariate-bicycle code, on which our decoder is 16 times more accurate than the real-time Relay decoder. We further show that the decoder scales: spread over several FPGAs or hardened into custom silicon, it becomes faster, more accurate, or able to decode larger codes. Classical hardware thus becomes a further resource, alongside qubits, that can be scaled to improve fault-tolerant quantum computers.

infographic.key_insight: Rapids co-designs a streaming neural decoder with FPGA hardware to deliver accurate, sub-microsecond quantum error correction.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Scaling classical decoding hardware alongside qubits offers a path to faster, more accurate fault-tolerant quantum computing.
method: Build the neural decoder from FPGA-efficient operations.
Train using the hardware’s integer arithmetic.
Scale across multiple FPGAs or harden into custom silicon.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports under 1 microsecond per syndrome round for a distance-19 surface code on one FPGA, a 240-fold lower logical error rate than existing real-time hardware decoders, and 16-fold better accuracy than Relay on the [[144,12,12]] bivariate-bicycle code.
infographic.watch_item: Multi-FPGA deployment must manage communication overhead while preserving throughput and low decision latency.
infographic.paper_title: Scaling classical hardware for accurate real-time quantum error correction

title: Non-Binary Detector Error Models
authors: Stefano Tinelli, Francisco Lázaro, Francisco García Herrero
abstract: A key challenge in fault-tolerant quantum error correction (QEC) is that the syndrome extraction circuits are themselves faulty. Such circuit-level noise is commonly described by a detector error model (DEM). In Stim and in almost all related works, DEMs are binary: every non-binary circuit error (e.g., CNOT gate), is decomposed into independent binary error mechanisms. In this work, we introduce non-binary DEMs, in which each fault location of the syndrome extraction circuit is modeled by one random variable over its original alphabet, e.g., the 16 two-qubit Pauli errors after a CNOT gate. We also propose a split-merge-regroup transformation that builds a compact non-binary DEM from any Clifford circuit by merging the error components that flip the same detectors and observables. Non-binary DEMs represent any Pauli channel exactly, whereas binary DEMs are exact only for channels that factorize into independent binary parts. When the channels factorize, we prove that binary and non-binary DEMs are equivalent under degenerate quantum maximum-a-posteriori (MAP) decoding, but not under quantum MAP decoding. Although the variables are non-binary, belief propagation (BP) still exchanges a single scalar message per edge. Our numerical results with surface, color and bivariate bicycle codes show that non-binary DEMs have two main advantages. First, their Tanner graphs have four to five times fewer edges, which is advantageous for hardware implementations. Second, their performance under BP, with and without OSD post-processing, is better than that of their binary counterparts, and BP with OSD runs up to $9.4\times$ faster in a CPU.

infographic.key_insight: Non-binary detector error models preserve each circuit fault’s original Pauli alphabet, representing arbitrary Pauli channels exactly while enabling more compact decoding graphs.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Tanner graphs with four to five times fewer edges could simplify decoder hardware, while BP with OSD post-processing achieved up to 9.4× CPU speedup in reported tests.
method: Model each fault location as one random variable over its original error alphabet.
Apply split-merge-regroup to merge components with identical detector and observable flips.
Decode using belief propagation with one scalar message per edge, optionally followed by OSD.
infographic.evidence_signal: Evaluations on surface, color and bivariate bicycle codes showed better BP performance, with and without OSD, than binary counterparts.
infographic.watch_item: Binary and non-binary models are proven equivalent only for factorizing channels under degenerate quantum MAP decoding, not under quantum MAP decoding.
infographic.paper_title: Non-Binary Detector Error Models

title: QFT-Based Hybrid PointNet-Quantum Neural Networks for LiDAR Point-Cloud Classification
authors: Anurag Kulkarni, Nouhaila Innan, Muhammad Shafique
abstract: Hybrid quantum-classical learning architectures provide a promising framework for integrating quantum feature transformations into complex data-processing tasks. Among these transformations, the Quantum Fourier Transform (QFT) offers a structured approach to feature processing, motivating an investigation of how its circuit configuration influences predictive performance, quantum resource requirements, and noise robustness. We present a hybrid PointNet-quantum neural network architecture for LiDAR point-cloud classification, combining classical feature extraction, amplitude encoding, and a variational quantum circuit. Five Fourier-processing configurations are systematically evaluated: No-QFT, Full-QFT-After, QFT-no-swap, IQFT-After, and Trainable-QFT. Experiments on KITTI, nuScenes, and PandaSet across three random seeds assess classification performance, class-level behavior, circuit complexity, and sensitivity to the IBM FakeManilaV2 noise model. Under ideal simulation, IQFT-After achieves the highest weighted F1-score on KITTI (0.857 $\pm$ 0.033), compared with 0.838 $\pm$ 0.023 for No-QFT. Removing the final SWAP gates in the QFT circuit reduces circuit complexity while preserving the Pauli-Z measurement features up to a fixed permutation that can be absorbed by the classification head. Under quantum noise, the circuit ranking changes, with IQFT-After exhibiting greater performance degradation and No-QFT and Trainable-QFT showing stronger robustness. Per-class analysis further identifies dataset-dependent differences in minority-class performance. These results demonstrate that Fourier-processing configuration influences both classification behavior and noise sensitivity, highlighting the role of circuit structure and hardware-aware evaluation in hybrid quantum learning for three-dimensional point-cloud data.

infographic.key_insight: Fourier-circuit configuration affects LiDAR classification accuracy and noise sensitivity: IQFT-After performs best on ideal KITTI simulations but degrades more under quantum noise.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Hardware-aware circuit selection matters, and removing final QFT SWAP gates reduces complexity while preserving Pauli-Z features up to a permutation absorbable by the classifier.
method: Combine PointNet feature extraction, amplitude encoding, and a variational quantum circuit.
Compare No-QFT, Full-QFT-After, QFT-no-swap, IQFT-After, and Trainable-QFT.
Evaluate classification, class-level behavior, circuit complexity, and simulated noise robustness.
infographic.evidence_signal: Tests on KITTI, nuScenes, and PandaSet across three seeds yielded ideal KITTI weighted F1 of 0.857 ± 0.033 for IQFT-After versus 0.838 ± 0.023 for No-QFT; IBM FakeManilaV2 noise changed the circuit ranking.
infographic.watch_item: Noise-model simulations do not establish real-hardware performance, and minority-class behavior varies by dataset.
infographic.paper_title: QFT-Based Hybrid PointNet-Quantum Neural Networks for LiDAR Point-Cloud Classification

title: Nonlinearity-preserving quantum simulation of flows in the early fault-tolerant regime
authors: Hansol Noh, Unam Oh, Sangkyu Baek, Doyeol, Ahn
abstract: Ensemble prediction of nonlinear dynamics propagates a probability density whose linear transport equation retains the nonlinear drift, but grid-dependent circuit costs leave end-to-end feasibility in early fault-tolerant quantum computing unresolved. We couple polynomial reduced-order models fitted by sparse identification of nonlinear dynamics to Walsh-synthesized Koopman-von Neumann (KvN) transport and surface-code resource estimation. At fixed model dimension and drift degree, per-step transport rotation counts scale polylogarithmically with cells per reduced coordinate. Balancing model accuracy against circuit costs makes reduced-model polynomial degree a design variable for early fault-tolerant quantum simulation. For a cylinder wake approaching saturation, preparation, propagation and sampling to 1% relative root-mean-square field error against the radial model are estimated to take 1.62 h on about 560,000 physical qubits. Estimated three-coordinate wake runtimes span hours to weeks below one million qubits. IBM hardware experiments demonstrate nonlinear radial KvN transport for this wake, using reference circuits to mitigate noise.

infographic.key_insight: Polynomial reduced-order models paired with quantum transport preserve nonlinear flow dynamics while making per-step rotation counts polylogarithmic in grid resolution at fixed model dimension and drift degree.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Choosing reduced-model polynomial degree to balance accuracy and circuit cost offers a design lever for early fault-tolerant quantum flow simulation.
method: Fit polynomial reduced-order models using sparse identification of nonlinear dynamics.
Implement Koopman–von Neumann transport with Walsh-synthesized quantum circuits.
Estimate end-to-end runtime and physical-qubit requirements using surface-code resources.
infographic.evidence_signal: For a cylinder wake approaching saturation, the study estimates 1.62 hours on about 560,000 physical qubits for 1% relative RMS field error against the radial model, and demonstrates nonlinear radial transport on IBM hardware with reference-circuit noise mitigation.
infographic.watch_item: The fault-tolerant runtimes are estimates, and the reported 1% error is measured against a reduced radial model rather than a full-flow reference.
infographic.paper_title: Nonlinearity-preserving quantum simulation of flows in the early fault-tolerant regime

title: The classical complexity of quantum state transmission
authors: Elna Svegborn, Alexander Bernal, Armin Tavakoli
abstract: Quantum communication provides a natural means to transmit quantum information, but how difficult is it to make such a transmission using only classical communication resources? We address this question by introducing classical communication models for quantum preparations and defining their minimum cost as the classical complexity. We prove that this complexity equals the amount of classical communication required to simulate quantum correlations in prepare-and-broadcast experiments, thus establishing a resource equivalence between quantum state transmission and quantum correlations. This calls for a general characterisation of the classical complexity of the noisy quantum state space, which we show grows exponentially with the quantum dimension and as a power-law in the inverse noise. It reveals the rapidly scaling fundamental cost of classical simulation. Moreover, we develop a toolbox of methods to certify classical complexity in quantum preparation devices, including an exact semidefinite-programming characterisation, analytical witnesses for symmetric preparations and convex programming scalable up to hundreds and sometimes thousands of qubit states. Our results establish classical complexity as a fundamental measure of quantum communication advantage, revealing the intrinsic cost of classically simulating quantum theory and providing practical tools for its certification.

infographic.key_insight: The classical communication cost of simulating quantum state transmission equals that of simulating prepare-and-broadcast quantum correlations, growing exponentially with quantum dimension and as a power law in inverse noise.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Classical complexity provides a resource benchmark for quantum communication advantage and tools to certify it in quantum preparation devices.
method: Define minimum-cost classical communication models for quantum preparations.
Prove resource equivalence with prepare-and-broadcast correlation simulation.
Certify complexity using semidefinite programming, analytical witnesses and scalable convex programming.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports theoretical scaling results, an exact semidefinite-programming characterisation and convex methods scalable to hundreds and sometimes thousands of qubit states.
infographic.watch_item: The abstract does not report hardware validation, and practical certification costs may depend on the preparation set and noise model.
infographic.paper_title: The classical complexity of quantum state transmission

title: Agentic MLIR-to-QIR Translation with Dual-Backend Testing: A Hybrid Deterministic and LLM Approach
authors: Sharmin Afrose, Vicente Leyton-Ortega, Narasinga Rao Miniskar, Elaine Wong, Travis S. Humble
abstract: Quantum frameworks each define their own Multi-Level Intermediate Representation (MLIR) dialect, so porting a circuit to a Quantum Intermediate Representation (QIR) runtime needs a hand-written pass per dialect. Our translator selects among three paths: a deterministic compiler path for known grammars (Catalyst and Quake), a large language model (LLM) agentic path for unseen dialects, and a repair path invoked when deterministic output fails testing. A dual-backend pipeline executes the source MLIR and generated QIR on independent simulators, comparing output distributions by total variation distance (TVD). For smaller open-weight models we replace retrieval-augmented generation with inline context engineering and add a guardrail-assembler that rebuilds valid QIR from incomplete output. Across 41 circuits spanning three dialects and 1-100 qubits, the deterministic path is gate-exact on all 70 circuit-dialect pairs, averaging above 95% TVD similarity (1-TVD). On an unseen fault-tolerant (FTQC) dialect, four of six models produce valid logical-level QIR on the first iteration.

infographic.key_insight: A hybrid deterministic and LLM-agent translator converts quantum MLIR dialects to QIR, using dual-backend testing to detect translation errors.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The approach could reduce hand-written compiler work when connecting new quantum dialects to QIR runtimes while retaining deterministic translation for known grammars.
method: Use deterministic translation for Catalyst and Quake, and LLM agents for unseen dialects or repair after failed testing.
Run source MLIR and generated QIR on independent simulators; compare output distributions using total variation distance (TVD).
Support smaller open-weight models with inline context and a guardrail assembler that reconstructs valid QIR from incomplete output.
infographic.evidence_signal: Across 41 circuits spanning three dialects and 1–100 qubits, deterministic translation was gate-exact on all 70 tested circuit–dialect pairs with average 1−TVD above 95%; four of six models generated valid logical-level QIR for an unseen FTQC dialect on the first iteration.
infographic.watch_item: Valid QIR and close simulated output distributions do not alone establish semantic correctness for arbitrary unseen dialects.
infographic.paper_title: Agentic MLIR-to-QIR Translation with Dual-Backend Testing: A Hybrid Deterministic and LLM Approach

title: Beyond Error Mitigation: Using Boosting for Noisy Quantum Machine Learning
authors: Anastasiia Lukianenko, Yash J. Patel, Nurbolat Kenbayev, Vedran Dunjko
abstract: Quantum error mitigation (QEM) can recover information about ideal quantum computations from noisy circuit executions, but may require a large sampling overhead. Fundamental lower bounds show that recovering noiseless observables without problem-specific information can require superpolynomially many samples, with exponential overhead for broad classes of noisy circuits. However, problem-specific information can reduce the number of samples needed to obtain the required answer. We investigate this possibility in supervised quantum machine learning, where labeled examples provide information about the function to be learned. Binary classification provides such a setting, since correct prediction depends on the sign and margin of the classifier output rather than on accurate reconstruction of every noiseless expectation value. We develop a theoretical and empirical framework for comparing boosting of noisy parameterized quantum circuits with probabilistic error cancellation (PEC), requiring both methods to reach the same learning target. For the specified circuit architectures under Pauli noise, we establish a common hypothesis-class complexity bound: matching empirical margin loss gives the same upper bound on expected classification risk. We derive resource criteria and evaluate AdaBoostR and Real AdaBoost in finite-shot teacher-student simulations across circuit depth and physical noise strength. Under the same classification-accuracy target, boosting requires fewer circuit executions as depth and noise increase. Boosting also achieves higher test accuracy than the corresponding reference. For the supervised-learning problems studied, these results demonstrate a task-dependent resource advantage: exploiting information retained in noisy outputs can avoid the cost of ideal-output reconstruction without sacrificing observed classification performance.

infographic.key_insight: Boosting noisy quantum classifiers can achieve the same classification-accuracy target with fewer circuit executions than probabilistic error cancellation, without reconstructing ideal quantum outputs.
infographic.engineering_relevance: For supervised quantum learning, task-aware ensembles offer a potential way to reduce sampling costs as circuit depth and physical noise increase.
method: Combine noisy parameterized quantum circuits using AdaBoostR and Real AdaBoost.
Compare boosting with probabilistic error cancellation at a matched learning target.
Establish a shared classification-risk bound from empirical margin loss for specified architectures under Pauli noise.
infographic.evidence_signal: Finite-shot teacher–student simulations across circuit depths and noise strengths showed lower execution costs at matched accuracy and higher test accuracy than the corresponding reference.
infographic.watch_item: The advantage is task-dependent and demonstrated for specified architectures and simulated noise; performance on hardware and broader datasets remains to be established.
infographic.paper_title: Beyond Error Mitigation: Using Boosting for Noisy Quantum Machine Learning

title: Residual-Algebraic Design of Symmetry-Preserving Variational Quantum Circuits
authors: Sahinur Reja
abstract: Symmetry-preserving (SP) variational quantum circuits restrict evolution to physically relevant sectors of Hilbert space, but symmetry preservation alone does not guarantee accessibility within those sectors. We show that a restricted generator set can possess a residual dynamical Lie algebra whose commutant further decomposes the target symmetry sector into invariant blocks. The associated block populations are conserved and impose a kinematic upper bound on the fidelity with a target state. We then invert this diagnostic into a circuit-design principle: candidate SP generators can be screened before variational optimization by asking whether they break the residual commutant, which invariant blocks they couple, and what adjoint module they generate under the residual algebra. For two orthogonal residual blocks we prove that a single elementary real inter-block rotation generates the full orthogonal algebra. We further derive a complex escape criterion: if the real and imaginary parts of an inter-block seed are independent over the residual intertwiner algebra, the generated module is the full complex coupling space and the enlarged algebra becomes special unitary. A connected residual-block graph yields a natural multi-block generalization and suggests minimum-cost spanning-tree circuit design. We demonstrate this design principle in the XXZ and Hubbard models, where residual-algebra screening identifies SP circuit extensions that remove the relevant accessibility obstructions. These examples establish a unified route from residual-symmetry diagnosis and fidelity bounds to predictive quantum circuit design.

infographic.key_insight: Symmetry-preserving quantum circuits can still be trapped in invariant subspaces, but residual-algebra analysis identifies added generators that unlock target-state accessibility.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Screening symmetry-preserving gates before optimization can reveal unreachable targets and guide circuit extensions that remove structural barriers.
method: Compute the residual algebra and its commutant to identify invariant blocks and fidelity bounds.
Screen added generators by the blocks they couple and the adjoint modules they generate.
Use real-rotation and complex-escape criteria to expand controllability; connect multiple blocks through a low-cost spanning tree.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports algebraic proofs and demonstrations in XXZ and Hubbard models, where screened circuit extensions remove identified accessibility obstructions.
infographic.watch_item: Removing algebraic accessibility barriers does not by itself guarantee shallow circuits, noise robustness, or successful variational optimization.
infographic.paper_title: Residual-Algebraic Design of Symmetry-Preserving Variational Quantum Circuits

title: Fast, in-place, and ancilla-free quantum algorithms for integer multiplication and inversion
authors: David Halpenny, Adithya Sireesh, Petros Wallden
abstract: Arithmetic operations are a fundamental building block in the design of quantum algorithms, with their implementation cost expected to have a significant impact on the viability of a wide variety of quantum applications. In this work, we present novel algorithms for a number of in-place quantum arithmetic operations that are highly efficient in terms of their space and gate count overheads compared to the current state-of-the-art. We show that in-place modular multiplication of integers, modulo a power of two, can be performed with either a classical or quantum odd multiplier using $O(n^{1+ε})$ gates and no ancilla qubits, for any $ε>0$. We then show that standard in-place integer multiplication can be performed with a non-zero classical or quantum multiplier using $O(n^{1+ε})$ gates for any $ε>0$, with no ancilla qubits required for the classical multiplier and a logarithmic number of ancilla qubits for the quantum. Using our quantum modular multiplication algorithm, we also show that in-place modular inversion, modulo a power of two, can be performed using $O(n^{1+ε})$ gates and no ancilla qubits, for any $ε>0$. To our knowledge, these are the first quantum algorithms achieving both subquadratic gate counts and sublinear ancilla counts for each of the considered in-place operations. All but one of these fast operations are optimal in terms of memory, only requiring enough space to store the output of the operation, which overwrites the input directly. We present our multiplication algorithms as consequences of a single unified theorem, which may find further application within quantum arithmetic.

infographic.key_insight: In-place quantum multiplication and modular inversion achieve O(n^(1+ε)) gate counts for any ε > 0, with zero ancillas in most cases.
infographic.engineering_relevance: These arithmetic primitives could reduce gate and workspace overheads in quantum applications while overwriting inputs directly with outputs.
method: Derive multiplication algorithms from a unified theorem.
Multiply modulo 2^n using odd classical or quantum multipliers without ancillas.
Extend to standard multiplication with nonzero multipliers and ancilla-free inversion modulo 2^n.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports theoretical complexity guarantees, including the first claimed combination of subquadratic gates and sublinear ancillas for these operations, but no empirical benchmarks.
infographic.watch_item: Standard multiplication with a quantum multiplier still requires logarithmically many ancillas, and practical gate constants are not specified in the abstract.
infographic.paper_title: Fast, in-place, and ancilla-free quantum algorithms for integer multiplication and inversion
